thinking: Read two integers from standard input, compute their sum, and output the result. The problem is a basic I/O warm-up that also encourages attention to the data range constraint.
summary: Always check the constraint bounds before selecting a data type; forming this habit early avoids overflow bugs later.

thinking: Four nested loops enumerate a, b, c, d subject to b <= c <= d to avoid duplicate permutations. The constraint naturally prunes the search space and eliminates the need for a deduplication set.
summary: Embedding order constraints directly in loop bounds is far more efficient than post-hoc deduplication with a set.

thinking: Brute-force search from d+1 to d+21252, checking whether each candidate simultaneously satisfies the three modulo conditions for physical, emotional, and intellectual peaks. The problem guarantees the answer lies within this range, so the upper bound is hard-coded.
summary: When the problem statement provides a concrete bound, use it directly for the loop limit rather than over-engineering a solution.

thinking: Read T groups of data; for each group, read N and then N integers, sort with std::sort, and output in ascending order. Pay attention to the output format: each result on its own line with no trailing space.
summary: The "first N-1 with spaces, last one with newline" pattern cleanly avoids trailing spaces without an inline conditional.

thinking: Enumerate all 12 coins under both the "heavy" and "light" assumptions, then verify each hypothesis against the three weighings. Only 24 total possibilities, so brute-force checking is simpler than any logical deduction chain.
summary: With only 12 x 2 = 24 possibilities, exhaustive verification is easier and less error-prone than manual reasoning.

thinking: Use the two-pointer technique on a sorted array: start one pointer at the left and another at the right, moving them inward based on whether the current sum is less than or greater than the target. This achieves O(n) time versus O(n^2) for the naive nested loop.
summary: Whenever the input array is sorted, consider two pointers first — the O(n) improvement over brute force is substantial.

thinking: Fix the first element and apply the two-pointer technique on the remaining subarray to find the other two. This reduces the triple loop to O(n^2) and is a natural extension of the two-sum pattern.
summary: The N-sum problem family follows a uniform template: fix outer variables, then use two pointers on the remainder.

thinking: Fix two outer indices, then use two pointers on the remaining segment to find the last two numbers. The four-layer loop collapses to O(n^3), following the same recursive structure as the two- and three-sum problems.
summary: N-sum is just an increasingly long chain of fixed outer loops with an invariant two-pointer core.

thinking: Recursively move n-1 disks from the source to the auxiliary peg using the destination as a buffer, move the largest disk directly to the destination, then move the n-1 disks from the auxiliary to the destination. The recursion handles all details automatically.
summary: Trust the recursion by reducing n disks to 1 disk plus n-1 disks; do not try to simulate every intermediate step mentally.

thinking: Identical recursive structure to Hanoi I, but the output must include each disk's number and the peg names are read from input rather than hard-coded as A, B, C.
summary: Custom peg names and disk numbering do not change the core recursion — they only add an extra parameter to pass along.

thinking: Standard DFS permutation template: maintain a used[] array to track which numbers are already placed, recurse to fill the next position, and backtrack by clearing the used flag when returning.
summary: DFS permutations follow a three-step pattern: mark, recurse, unmark — a foundational technique for all backtracking problems.

thinking: Same DFS template as numeric permutations, but the input characters may not be sorted initially, so sort the string first to guarantee lexicographic output order.
summary: Character permutations are identical to numeric permutations; the only trap is forgetting to sort the input string before DFS.

thinking: Classic N-Queens DFS: place one queen per row and check column and diagonal conflicts against all previously placed queens. When the row index difference equals the column index difference, they share a diagonal.
summary: N-Queens is a permutation problem with an extra diagonal constraint: |set[j] - i| == |j - k| detects same-diagonal placement concisely.

thinking: Since the board is fixed at 8x8 with only 92 distinct solutions, precompute all solutions via DFS once and store them as strings. Sort the result list and answer each query by direct index lookup — O(1) per query regardless of how many times the program is asked.
summary: For fixed-size combinatorial problems, precomputing all solutions at startup turns repeated queries into constant-time lookups.

thinking: Same N-Queens logic but the output now uses '.' for empty squares and 'Q' for queens. Three boolean arrays (col, diag1, diag2) provide O(1) conflict checks instead of the loop-based approach used in the previous version.
summary: Using three boolean marker arrays instead of a loop to check conflicts is a clean space-for-time optimization common in search problems.

thinking: The number of ways to climb N stairs equals the N-th Fibonacci number: from step N you can only have come from N-1 or N-2, giving f(N) = f(N-1) + f(N-2). A simple recursive function suffices.
summary: Climbing stairs is Fibonacci in disguise — get the base cases (f(0)=1, f(1)=1, f(2)=2) right and the recursion writes itself.

thinking: Classic integer partition problem solved recursively: either every plate gets at least one apple (reduce apple count) or one plate is left empty (reduce plate count). The base case is when apples reach zero, returning 1.
summary: The key insight is to decompose the problem into "all plates get one" and "one plate stays empty" — two simple recursive branches.

thinking: Prefix expressions are naturally evaluated with recursion: cin reads a token; if it is an operator, recursively evaluate the left and right operands; otherwise, convert the token to a float with atof and return it.
summary: Prefix expression evaluation is a perfect fit for recursion — cin's whitespace-delimited input matches the structure exactly.

thinking: Extract the binary representation of N, then for each set bit, recursively format the exponent the same way. The exponent 1 is the special case where parentheses are omitted (just "2"), while exponent 0 becomes "2(0)".
summary: Binary decomposition plus recursive exponent formatting; the special case for 2^1 where parentheses are dropped is easy to overlook.

thinking: Each integer from 1 to n has two choices: selected or not. DFS explores both branches for every number, generating all 2^n subsets. With n <= 15, exponential enumeration is trivial.
summary: Subset enumeration via DFS is the simplest backtracking template — each element just branches on take or skip.

thinking: Combinatorial enumeration uses DFS with a start parameter: at each position, only pick numbers greater than the previously chosen one, guaranteeing ascending order and no duplicate combinations. This naturally produces lexicographic output.
summary: The one-parameter difference between combination and permutation DFS is the start index versus a used[] array — mixing them up causes painful debugging.

thinking: Full permutation enumeration by filling positions one by one: a used[] array marks numbers already placed, and each recursive call picks an unused number for the current slot, backtracking on return.
summary: Permutation DFS uses a used[] array; combination DFS uses a start parameter. Remembering to unmark on backtrack is critical for both.

thinking: With only '+' and '*' operators and '*' having higher precedence, maintain a cur variable that accumulates the current multiplicative segment. When '+' is encountered, add cur to the answer and reset cur. A single pass suffices — no stack needed.
summary: For expressions with only two precedence levels, a running multiplicative-segment variable is simpler than a full operator stack.

thinking: Each button press affects itself and its immediate neighbors; pressing a button more than once is redundant. There are only 2 possibilities for the first button (press or not), and once that is fixed, every subsequent button's state is forced by whether the previous position matches the target. O(n) for the whole check.
summary: Enumerating just the first button's state (2 cases) and propagating deterministically is a classic puzzle-solving technique — find the "driving variable."

thinking: Enumerate all 64 possible press configurations for the first row of the 5x6 grid. For each configuration, the press pattern for subsequent rows is forced: if a light at (i, j) is still on, the button at (i+1, j) must be pressed to turn it off. Finally check whether the last row is completely dark.
summary: Enumerating the first row reduces a 2^30 search space to 2^6, and the rest follows deterministically — identify the right driving variable.

thinking: Each of the 9 operations can be applied at most 3 times (4 rotations return to the starting position). Brute-force all 4^9 = 262,144 combinations, verify that all clocks point to 12, and select the shortest sequence (with smallest lexicographic order on ties).
summary: 4^9 is only ~260k — brute force is fine. The critical detail is that each operation cycles every 4 presses, so the range is 0-3, not arbitrary.

thinking: Recursively pick any two numbers from the current list, combine them with +, -, *, or /, and place the result back. Repeat until only one number remains, then check whether it equals 24. The recursion naturally accounts for all parenthesizations without explicit bracket enumeration.
summary: The "pick two and merge" recursion implicitly generates every parenthesization — no need to enumerate bracket positions explicitly.

thinking: Implement quicksort with the classic do-while two-pointer partition: choose a pivot from the middle, swap elements on the wrong sides, then recursively sort the two halves. With n up to 100,000, O(n log n) is required; bubble sort would time out.
summary: The do-while implementation of quicksort partition is cleaner than while(true) versions, but the recursive call must use j, not i, to avoid infinite recursion.

thinking: Full quicksort followed by direct index access to the k-th element suffices for n <= 100,000. Although the intended technique is quickselect (partitioning only the relevant half), full sort at O(n log n) is still fast enough.
summary: Quickselect can find the k-th smallest element in O(n), but when n is moderate, full sort plus array access is simpler and equally acceptable.

thinking: Sort the array and output the last k elements in reverse order. Pay attention to the input format: n on the first line, the array on the second line, and k on the third line, not all on one line.
summary: This is a straightforward sorting problem — the only challenge is reading the input correctly when n and k are on separate lines.

thinking: Merge sort recursively divides the array into halves, sorts each half, and merges the two sorted subarrays with a two-pointer pass. It is a stable O(n log n) algorithm that always uses the same amount of extra space.
summary: After merging, the temporary array must be copied back to the original segment — forgetting this step breaks the whole sort.

thinking: Count inversions during merge sort: whenever an element from the right half is taken before an element from the left half, all remaining elements in the left half form an inversion with it. Accumulate cnt += mid - i + 1.
summary: Counting inversions adds just one line to merge sort, but the result must be stored in long long to avoid overflow.

thinking: Since the array is not guaranteed to be sorted, use std::find for linear search. For each query, find returns an iterator which can be converted to an index via std::distance, or the result is -1 if not found.
summary: Read the input order carefully: N, then the array, then T, then the T queries — the format is not always what it first appears to be.

thinking: On a sorted array, use lower_bound to find the first occurrence of the target and upper_bound-1 to find the last occurrence. Both operations are O(log n) and together give the full range of positions for duplicate values.
summary: The condition l > r is a concise way to detect when the target is absent, and lower_bound/upper_bound form a universal binary-search range query.

thinking: The function f(x) changes sign between 5 and 6 (f(5) < 0, f(6) > 0), so the root lies in [5, 6]. Binary search halves the interval until the width falls below 1e-10, then output the midpoint with 9 decimal places.
summary: Bisection for root-finding uses the sign of f(mid) relative to f(l) to decide which half to keep — a loop is simpler and clearer than recursion here.

thinking: Compute the cube root of a floating-point number by binary search over the range [-100, 100]. At each step, compare mid^3 with the target and adjust the interval accordingly, stopping when the interval width is below 1e-8.
summary: Cube root via binary search is straightforward — just compare mid^3 against n. Remember that negative numbers also have valid cube roots.

thinking: Binary search on the answer combined with a greedy validation: given a budget, greedily group consecutive days into segments. If any single day exceeds the budget or the total number of groups exceeds M, the budget is insufficient.
summary: The "minimize the maximum" pattern always suggests binary search on the answer with a greedy check. The search bounds are [max(a), sum(a)].

thinking: Binary search on the volume per person. For a candidate volume, compute how many slices each cylindrical cake can yield (integer division of its volume by the candidate). If the total slice count reaches at least F+1 (friends plus Link himself), the volume is feasible.
summary: Remember that Link himself also gets a slice, so the head count is F+1, not F. Use a fixed number of iterations (e.g., 100) for the binary search to avoid floating-point precision traps.

thinking: DFS backtracking on a grid where movement is restricted to down, left, and right. Visited cells are marked to prevent revisiting, and the mark is cleared upon backtracking. With n <= 20, the DFS completes within time.
summary: Backtracking requires restoring the visited state when returning from recursion; skipping this step produces wildly incorrect counts.

thinking: Flood-fill DFS from the starting position '@', expanding into all four-directionally adjacent '.' cells and counting the reachable area. Visited cells are overwritten with '#' to serve as an implicit visited array.
summary: Modifying the grid in-place to mark visited cells avoids a separate visited[][] array — just remember to re-read the grid for each test case.

thinking: DFS backtracking to find a Hamiltonian path on a rectangular chessboard with knight moves. The eight move offsets are arranged in lexicographic order so that the first complete path found is automatically the smallest in dictionary order.
summary: The order of the eight knight-move vectors determines the lexicographic output order — arrange them carefully before starting DFS.

thinking: DFS that enumerates the radius and height of each cake layer from bottom to top. Three pruning strategies are essential: minimum remaining volume, maximum possible volume, and current surface area lower bound. Without all three, the search will time out.
code:
if (sumV + minV[layer] > V) return;     // 剩余层即使取最小也已超体积
if (sumS + minS[layer] >= ans) return;  // 表面积已经比已知最优大
if (sumV + maxV < V) return;            // 剩余层取最大也不够体积
summary: DFS with pruning for combinatorial optimization problems often requires multiple bounds — min-volume, max-volume, and optimal-area cutoffs all needed here.

thinking: Memoized recursive search over rectangular subdivisions: try every possible horizontal or vertical cut and every possible distribution of the remaining pieces among the two resulting rectangles. The result is the minimum of the maximum sub-rectangle areas.
summary: The DP state (width, height, pieces) is large enough that memoization is essential. Both cut position and piece allocation must be enumerated.

thinking: Repeatedly apply the lowbit operation x &= x - 1, which removes the lowest set bit in each iteration, and count how many times it can be applied before x reaches zero. This is faster than checking each bit position individually.
summary: The expression x &= x - 1 is the classic trick for counting set bits; it works correctly for negative integers in two's complement representation.

thinking: Use lowbit (n & -n) to extract the lowest set bit as a power of two, then look up its position in a precomputed log2 table. This combination gives O(1) bit position queries without looping over individual bits.
summary: lowbit extracts the lowest set bit in one operation; combined with a lookup table, finding its position is O(1).

thinking: Verify a proposed Sudoku solution against three rules: (1) consistency with the initial fixed digits in the starting matrix, (2) no duplicate digits in any row or column, and (3) no duplicate in any 3x3 block. All three checks must pass.
code:
if(a[i][j]!=0 && a[i][j]!=t) return false;  // 跟已知初始位冲突直接判假
// check_row + check_col + check_block 三重校验，缺一不可
summary: Sudoku validation boils down to three independent checks — row, column, and block — plus the initial constraint. Each is straightforward, but all must pass.

thinking: Standard Sudoku solver using DFS: for each empty cell, try digits 1-9 and use three boolean arrays tracking which digits have been used in the current row, column, and 3x3 block. When a digit is placed, update all three arrays and recurse to the next cell.
summary: The three boolean arrays (row, column, block) are the basic data structure for DFS Sudoku solvers; they are updated and reverted together on backtracking.

thinking: Use bitwise state to represent available digits in each row, column, and block (9 bits per line). lowbit enumerates candidates, and the cell with the fewest candidates is chosen for branching first — this ordering dramatically prunes the search tree.
code:
int t=ones[get(i,j)];  // 当前格子可用候选数个数
if(t<minv) { minv=t; x=i,y=j; }  // 选候选最少的格子，剪枝效率最高
for(int i=get(x,y);i;i-=lowbit(i)) {  // lowbit枚举所有候选数字
    int t=LOG[lowbit(i)];
summary: Three speedup techniques for Sudoku DFS: bitmask states, lowbit enumeration, and minimum-remaining-values heuristic. The last one does the most work.

thinking: Extends LinK47 with a weighted scoring system: each cell's contribution is its digit multiplied by a weight that decreases radially from the center (10 at center to 6 at edges). Instead of stopping at any valid solution, search all solutions and return the maximum total score.
summary: Target-shaped Sudoku adds a distance-based weight per cell; the search must explore all solutions (not just the first) and track the maximum score.

thinking: Generalize the 9x9 bitmask Sudoku solver to 16x16 with 4x4 blocks. The bit count increases from 9 to 16, but the strategy — bitmask states, lowbit enumeration, minimum-remaining-values heuristic — scales directly.
summary: The jump from 9x9 to 16x16 Sudoku requires no new algorithms — just wider bitmasks. The same optimization techniques transfer directly.

thinking: Same as LinK49: 16x16 letter Sudoku solver using bitwise states, lowbit candidate extraction, and minimum-remaining-values ordering. Without the candidate-ordering heuristic, a naive DFS will time out even with bitmask optimizations.
summary: Bitmask optimizations alone are insufficient for 16x16 Sudoku — the minimum-remaining-values heuristic is the decisive optimization.

thinking: BFS flood-fill to count the size of the connected component reachable from '@'. The queue processes cells in FIFO order, marking visited cells as '#' and counting each cell popped. This is the BFS equivalent of the DFS flood-fill in LinK39.
summary: BFS flood-fill follows the same principle as the DFS version. Pay attention to the input order: the first integer is column count W, then row count H.

thinking: BFS with an additional digit-sum constraint: a cell at (i, j) can only be entered if the sum of its row and column digits is <= k. The rest is a standard 4-direction connectivity count.
summary: The digit-sum function must handle coordinate values of 0 correctly (the while loop simply does not execute, returning 0). Also handle the edge case where m or n is 0.

thinking: Single-source BFS expanding in 8 directions (king moves). The distance array records how many days each clean cell takes to become infected. The answer is the maximum distance among all reachable cells — the time required for complete saturation.
summary: BFS layer expansion naturally measures the infection time; the answer is simply the maximum distance value, which corresponds to the last BFS layer reached.

thinking: Standard knight BFS on a grid with obstacles: the knight moves in the 8 L-shaped offsets typical of chess knights. Search from 'K' to 'H', tracking distance (step count). The input lists columns first, then rows.
summary: Knight BFS is a classic shortest-path problem. The 8 move offsets must cover all L-shapes, and the column/row input order is the opposite of what many expect.

thinking: Multi-source BFS: all '1' cells are enqueued initially with distance 0, then the BFS expands outward in four directions. Each '0' cell receives the distance to its nearest '1' cell. This is far more efficient than running BFS from each source individually.
summary: Multi-source BFS initializes the queue with all source nodes simultaneously — it computes distances to the nearest source in a single pass.

thinking: A rolling block has three orientations (standing, lying horizontally, lying vertically), so the state is (x, y, lie). Precompute a 3x4x3 transition table that maps each (orientation, direction) to the new position and orientation. BFS on this state space finds the minimum number of rolls.
summary: Building the orientation-transition table for each of the 3 states x 4 directions is the hardest part; once the table is correct, the BFS is standard.

thinking: For dense graphs (n <= 500), the O(n^2) plain Dijkstra using an adjacency matrix is sufficient. Maintain a dist array and a visited set, repeatedly extracting the unvisited node with the smallest distance and relaxing its outgoing edges.
summary: Plain Dijkstra works well for small dense graphs (n up to ~10^4 edges). Use the heap-optimized version when n exceeds 10^5 or the graph is sparse.

thinking: For sparse graphs with up to 10^5 nodes and edges, use heap-optimized Dijkstra. An adjacency list stores the graph, and a priority_queue (min-heap via greater) extracts the node with the smallest distance. Relax edges and push improved distances back into the heap.
summary: Heap-optimized Dijkstra uses a priority_queue with greater to simulate a min-heap. The pair stores (distance, node) — reversing the order would break sorting.

thinking: Model the circuit as a grid of (R+1) x (C+1) nodes. Each diagonal wire corresponds to either cost 0 (if it already matches the desired direction) or cost 1 (if it needs rotating). Use a 0-1 BFS (deque) to find the minimum number of rotations needed to connect the top-left and bottom-right nodes.
summary: 0-1 BFS replaces the priority queue with a deque: cost-0 edges push front, cost-1 edges push back. The node count is (R+1)*(C+1), not R*C.

thinking: Kahn's algorithm for topological sort: enqueue all nodes with indegree 0, repeatedly pop a node, decrement the indegree of its outgoing neighbors, and enqueue any neighbor whose indegree reaches zero. If all nodes are processed, the output order is a valid topological order; otherwise, the graph contains a cycle.
summary: Kahn's algorithm processes nodes with indegree zero iteratively. Check whether the number of processed nodes equals n to detect cycles.

thinking: Model the problem as a state-space graph where each state is (city, fuel_remaining). Two transitions exist: buying one unit of fuel at the current city's price (fuel decreases, cost increases by price) or driving along an edge (fuel decreases by the edge's consumption). Run Dijkstra over this state space.
summary: State-space Dijkstra augments the node with additional dimensions (here, fuel level). The two transition types correspond to filling gas and traveling along edges.

thinking: Bottom-up DP starting from the second-to-last row: for each cell, add the larger of the cell directly below and the cell below-right. When the top is reached, f[1][1] holds the maximum path sum.
summary: Bottom-up DP eliminates boundary checks: each cell only needs the two values below it, making the code simpler than a top-down approach.

thinking: 0/1 Knapsack DP: for each item, f[i][j] inherits from f[i-1][j] (skip) or takes f[i-1][j-v[i]]+w[i] (take). The 2D version makes the recurrence explicit; the 1D optimized version requires j to iterate downward to prevent an item from being used multiple times.
summary: 0/1 Knapsack is the foundation of all knapsack variants. The key implementation detail is the downward loop direction in the 1D optimization.

thinking: Unbounded knapsack: each item can be used any number of times. The recurrence is f[i][j] = max(f[i-1][j], f[i][j-v[i]] + w[i]), where the second term references the same row i (not i-1), reflecting that the item is available again. The 1D version iterates j forward.
summary: The difference between 0/1 and unbounded knapsack in 1D is the loop direction for j: forward for unbounded (reuse allowed), backward for 0/1 (use once).

thinking: Bounded knapsack with small constraints (n, V, s <= 100): use three nested loops enumerating each possible item count k from 0 to s[i]. This direct O(N*V*max_s) approach is simple and sufficient when all quantities are small.
summary: The triple-loop approach is fine for small constraints but must be replaced with binary or monotonic-queue optimization when item counts grow beyond ~100.

thinking: Binary optimization for bounded knapsack: decompose each item with count s into O(log s) groups with sizes 1, 2, 4, ..., plus any remainder. Each group becomes a single 0/1 item. This reduces the overall complexity to O(N * V * log s).
summary: Binary splitting converts any bounded knapsack into a 0/1 knapsack with O(log s) items per original type — a fundamental and reusable optimization pattern.

thinking: Group knapsack: within each group, pick at most one item. The outer loop iterates groups, the capacity loop runs backward (like 0/1), and an inner loop evaluates all items in the group to find the best choice for each capacity.
summary: Although the code structure resembles multiple knapsack, the semantics differ: group knapsack picks at most one per group, while multiple knapsack picks up to s copies of the same item.

thinking: Mixed knapsack handles three item types in a single pass: 0/1 items (s == -1, treat as s = 1 for loop uniformity), unbounded items (s == 0, forward loop), and bounded items (s > 0, binary split then 0/1 processing). All updates share the same 1D f array.
summary: Mixed knapsack is a case-by-case combination of the three standard variants; the critical distinction is forward loop for unbounded versus backward for 0/1.

thinking: Simple 2D grid DP: each cell (i, j) can only be reached from (i-1, j) above or (i, j-1) left. The value at (i, j) is the grid value plus the larger of the two incoming paths. Process rows top-to-bottom, columns left-to-right.
summary: 2D grid DP is the most intuitive DP model — just add the current cell's value to the best incoming direction, with zero-initialized boundaries handling edges naturally.

thinking: The 2N-1 time limit forbids backtracking, meaning movement is effectively restricted to right and down only. This reduces the problem to the standard 2D grid DP (min-path variant) from the top-left to bottom-right corner.
summary: The 2N-1 constraint is a hint in disguise: it means no backtracking is possible, making the problem a standard right/down grid DP.

thinking: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS), O(n^2) version: f[i] records the length of the longest subsequence ending at position i. For each i, scan all j < i and extend f[j] if a[j] < a[i]. The answer is the maximum over all f[i].
summary: The O(n^2) LIS initializes f[i] = 1 (each element is a subsequence of length 1 on its own) before checking for extensions.

thinking: For n up to 100,000, use the O(n log n) greedy + binary search LIS: maintain q[len] as the smallest possible tail value for increasing subsequences of length len. For each a[i], binary search for the largest q[l] < a[i], then update q[l+1] = a[i].
summary: The q array stores the minimum possible ending value for each subsequence length, not the actual subsequence — understanding this distinction is key to applying the technique elsewhere.

thinking: Two problems in one: (1) the maximum number of interceptable missiles is the length of the longest non-increasing subsequence, computed via O(n^2) DP; (2) the minimum number of interception systems needed equals the length of the longest increasing subsequence (Dilworth's theorem), computable greedily in O(n log n).
summary: The second question reduces to the LIS length via Dilworth's theorem, so the O(n log n) greedy LIS code can answer both parts.

thinking: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) 2D DP: f[i][j] represents the LCS length of the first i characters of string A and the first j characters of string B. When characters match, f[i][j] = f[i-1][j-1] + 1; otherwise, f[i][j] = max(f[i-1][j], f[i][j-1]).
summary: LCS has exactly two transition branches: match together (diagonal +1) or carry forward the larger of the left/up neighbors. The code is remarkably compact.

thinking: Interval DP for merging adjacent stone piles: f[i][j] is the minimum cost to merge piles i through j. Enumerate the split point k between i and j, and the cost is f[i][k] + f[k+1][j] + the sum of weights in [i, j]. Process intervals by increasing length.
summary: Interval DP must iterate by segment length (not by left index), because a large interval depends on smaller intervals already being computed.

thinking: With a fixed in-order traversal, the problem reduces to interval DP enumerating the root of each subtree. For segment [l, r], try every k as the root; the total score is left_subtree_score * right_subtree_score + w[k], with empty subtrees treated as score 1. Also record root positions to reconstruct the pre-order traversal.
summary: The empty-subtree base case (score = 1) is easy to miss. Simultaneously storing the optimal root in a separate table enables recursive output of the tree structure.

thinking: Tree DP with two states per node: f[u][0] is the maximum happiness of the subtree when u does not attend, and f[u][1] when u does attend. If u attends, none of its children can attend; if u does not, children may attend or not. A post-order DFS computes the results bottom-up.
summary: Tree DP follows a uniform pattern: compute children first (post-order DFS), then combine results at the parent using the 0/1 attendance state.
